slides.title: Take every transformation mark on your paper
slides.prompt: A shape on a grid can only be moved in four ways, and describing each move earns marks in a fixed pattern every time. By the end of this lesson you will have banked 29 marks of real exam answers, four of them taken from actual past papers.

children.content: SLIDE
FLIP
SPIN
RESIZE

slides.title: Match each move to its proper name

interaction.hint: Translation slides, reflection flips, rotation spins, and enlargement resizes.

config.prompt: Drag each name onto the move it describes.

slides.title: Quick check before we dig in

interaction.hint: Only one of the four moves can turn a shape into its mirror image.

config.prompt: A triangle is moved, and its image is the same size but faces the opposite way round, like the view in a mirror. Which move was it?

options.whyWrong: A rotation turns the shape but never produces a mirror image. The corner labels still run round the shape the same way.
A translation only slides the shape along. It cannot make the shape face the other way.
An enlargement changes the size, and this image is exactly the same size as the object.

config.successText: Only a reflection produces a mirror image. Spotting a flipped shape is exactly how you will recognise reflections on the paper.

visual.content:
transformation 1 of 4
Translation

Sliding the shape without turning or flipping it. Every point moves the same amount, in the same direction.

Worth 2 marks when described: one for the word translation, one for the column vector. Writing the vector like a coordinate pair costs the second mark.

slides.title: Translation: drag the triangle anywhere
slides.prompt: Drag the triangle anywhere and watch the readout. Every point slides by the same amount, and that amount is written as a column vector.

slides.title: How to translate a point, step by step

config.title: How to translate a point, step by step
config.prompt: Top number = shift along x. Bottom number = shift along y. Walk through one, then drag the point yourself.

interaction.hint: Drag the yellow tip until the column vector reads $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$.

config.prompt: Drag until the image lands on the pink outline. Shift = $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$.
config.successText: Every point moved by $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$. That's the entire description.

config.title: How to find a column vector
config.prompt: Walk through the method one step at a time. Then drag the image at the end and watch the vector update.

interaction.hint: Subtract: image minus object. The order matters.

config.prompt: A point $(2, -1)$ has been translated to $(-3, 4)$. The column vector is...

options.whyWrong: You did object minus image. Always image minus object.
You used the image coordinates as the vector. The vector is the SHIFT, not the destination.
Those are the object coordinates, not the shift.

config.successText: $(-3 - 2,\ 4 - (-1)) = (-5, 5)$. Image minus object, always.

options.whyWrong: That is the everyday word. The examiner only accepts the proper name, which is translation.
A reflection would flip the triangle over. This one still points the same way.
A rotation would turn the triangle. This one has kept its angle and simply moved.
The numbers are upside down. The top number is always the sideways move.
Written in a row it reads as a coordinate. The vector must be written as a column.
That vector points up and to the left, but pink sits down and to the right of blue.

transformation 2 of 4
Reflection

Flipping the shape across a line, like in a mirror. The shape stays the same size, but its left and right swap.

Worth 2 marks when described: one for the word reflection, one for the equation of the mirror line. Vague words like the diagonal line earn nothing.

interaction.hint: The image sits exactly as far behind the mirror as $P$ sits in front of it.

config.prompt: The yellow line is a mirror. Tap the square where the mirror image of $P$ lands. A wrong guess costs nothing.
config.successText: The coordinates swapped over: $(4, 1)$ reflected to $(1, 4)$. Reflecting in $y = x$ always swaps the two coordinates. Now take the mirror for a spin.

slides.title: Reflection: drag the mirror line
slides.prompt: Every point flips to the other side of a line. Drag the yellow handles to move the mirror.

slides.title: How to reflect a point, step by step

config.title: How to reflect a point, step by step
config.prompt: Every point is the same perpendicular distance from the mirror as its image, just on the other side. Watch one, then drag your own point.

slides.title: Set the mirror to land on the pink ghost

interaction.hint: The pink ghost is directly below blue. The mirror is the horizontal axis.

config.prompt: Drag the mirror so blue reflects onto the pink outline. The mirror: $y = 0$ (the $x$-axis).
config.successText: $y = 0$ is the $x$-axis. Reflecting flips the sign of $y$ on every point.

config.prompt: Reflect $P\ (3, 5)$ in the yellow mirror $y = x$. Tap the image.
config.successText: Reflecting in $y = x$ just swaps the two coordinates. $(3, 5) \to (5, 3)$.

slides.title: Words don't earn marks. Equations do.

config.prompt: Two students describe the same reflection. Which one earns the mark?

options.whyWrong: Words don't earn the mark. The examiner needs the equation of the mirror line.

config.successText: Always give the mirror as an equation: $y = x$, $y = -x$, $x = 0$, $y = 0$. Never words.

interaction.hint: One of the two answers could mean several different lines. The examiner needs to know exactly which line.

slides.title: After a reflection, orientation reverses
slides.prompt:
Both triangles are exactly the same size and shape. The maths word for this is congruent.

Notice the labels. On the blue triangle, A then B then C goes clockwise. On the pink triangle, A' then B' then C' goes the other way, anticlockwise. A reflection always reverses the order of the labels. Hold your right hand up to a mirror and it looks like a left hand.

Spinning the shape around a fixed point. To describe it: how far, which way, and where.

Worth 3 marks when described: the word, the angle with its direction, and the centre. The most dropped mark on this topic is forgetting to say clockwise or anticlockwise.

interaction.hint: Imagine the grid stuck to a wheel that turns a quarter of the way round, against the clock.

config.prompt: Spin the grid a quarter turn anticlockwise about the yellow centre. Tap the square where $P$ ends up.
config.successText: $(3, 1)$ swings round to $(-1, 3)$. A quarter turn anticlockwise sends every point $(x, y)$ to $(-y, x)$. Now take the controls and test it.

slides.title: Rotation: drag the centre, drag the angle
slides.prompt: Three things describe any rotation: a point to spin around, how far to spin, and which way to spin.

interaction.hint: Centre at origin. Drag the angle handle a quarter-turn anticlockwise.

config.prompt: Rotate $90°$ anticlockwise about $(0, 0)$. Match the pink outline.
config.successText: $90°$ ACW about the origin: $(x, y) \to (-y, x)$.

slides.title: How to find the centre of a 90° rotation

config.title: How to find the centre of a 90° rotation
config.prompt: Given an object and its 90° rotated image, find the centre using perpendicular bisectors. Two bisectors meet at the centre.

slides.title: How to find the centre of a 180° rotation

config.title: How to find the centre of a 180° rotation
config.prompt: For 180°, the centre is just the midpoint of any vertex-image pair. No bisectors needed.

slides.title: What three things describe a rotation?

interaction.hint: Where to spin around, how far, which way.

config.prompt: What three things do you need to fully describe a rotation?

options.whyWrong: Mirror lines are for reflections, not rotations.
Scale factor is for enlargements, not rotations.
Column vectors are for translations. Rotations have a centre, not a vector.

config.successText: Centre + angle + direction. Drop any one of those and you lose a mark.

interaction.hint: Centre is where it spun around. Angle is how far. Direction is which way.

config.prompt: Fill in the three slots from the tiles below.
config.successText: Rotation, $90°$ anticlockwise, centre $(0, 0)$.

interaction.hint: A full turn is $360°$. Subtract from a full turn to flip direction.

options.whyWrong: That is the everyday word. The examiner only accepts the proper name, which is rotation.
Try to place a single mirror line between blue and pink and the corners never match up.
Both triangles are the same size, so nothing has been scaled.
Follow one corner: $(4, 1)$ travels up and round to $(-1, 4)$, which is against the clock.
A half turn would send $(4, 1)$ to $(-4, -1)$, into the bottom half of the grid.
The centre of a rotation stays where it is, but $(1, 1)$ has moved to $(-1, 1)$.
Every rotation needs a centre. Leave it out and you lose one of the three marks.

config.successText: Rotation, $90°$ anticlockwise, centre $(0, 0)$. Three pieces of information, and each one earns a mark.

judgments.explain: The proper word is there, so the first mark is safe.
judgments.whyWrong: The candidate wrote the exact word the scheme wants, so that mark is earned.

judgments.label: the angle with its direction
judgments.explain: $90°$ alone is not enough. Clockwise and anticlockwise give different images, so the direction is part of this mark.
judgments.whyWrong: Read line 2 again and ask: could an examiner tell which way the triangle turned?

judgments.label: the centre
judgments.explain: The centre is given as exact coordinates, exactly as required.
judgments.whyWrong: Look at line 3: the centre is stated precisely, so that mark stands.

config.faultExplain: One missing word cost the mark: it needed $90°$ anticlockwise. Forgetting the direction is the most dropped mark on this whole topic.
config.successText: Two out of three. Marking someone else’s answer is the fastest way to stop losing this mark yourself.

transformation 4 of 4
Enlargement

Stretching or shrinking the shape away from a fixed point. The only move that changes size.

Worth 3 marks when described: the word, the scale factor, and the centre. Fractional and negative scale factors appear often, so read the diagram carefully.

interaction.hint: Distances from the centre double when $k = 2$.

config.successText: $k = 2$: every distance from the centre doubled.

interaction.hint: Lengths scale by $k$. Areas scale by $k^2$, so square the scale factor.

config.prompt: After an enlargement with scale factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$, the image area is...

options.whyWrong: Half is what happens to lengths. Areas use $k^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}$.
Both wrong direction and wrong factor.

options.text: one quarter of the object area

options.whyWrong: Only if $k = 1$. Here $k = \tfrac{1}{2}$, so area must change.

config.successText: Areas scale by $k^2$. $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}$. Volume would be $k^3 = \tfrac{1}{8}$.

slides.title: Negative $k$ flips through the centre
slides.prompt:
A negative scale factor does two jobs at once. The number $2$ makes the new shape twice as big. The minus sign sends it to the opposite side of the centre.

Draw a line from each corner of the object through the centre, and the matching corner of the image lands on it. Three corners, three lines, all crossing at the centre.

visual.content:
two moves in a row
Combining moves

Doing one move, then another. The two together often make a single, different move.

Some questions chain two moves together and ask for the single move that replaces them. Two rules cover every case you will meet.

slides.title: Two parallel mirrors give a translation

config.title: Two parallel mirrors give a translation
config.prompt: Walk through the two reflections in order. The two parallel mirrors combine into one translation.

slides.title: Two intersecting mirrors give a rotation

config.title: Two intersecting mirrors give a rotation
config.prompt: Walk through the two reflections in order. The two intersecting mirrors combine into one rotation.

slides.title: Which single move replaces the pair?

interaction.hint: Crossing mirrors and parallel mirrors combine into different moves. This pair crosses.

config.prompt: A shape is reflected in one mirror, then in a second mirror that crosses the first. What single move replaces the pair?

options.whyWrong: That is what happens when the two mirrors are parallel. These two cross.
Two flips cancel the mirror-image effect, so the final shape faces the same way as the original. One reflection cannot do that.
Reflections never change the size of a shape, so no enlargement is involved.

config.successText: Two crossing mirrors combine into one rotation about the point where they cross. If the mirrors were parallel instead, the pair would combine into a translation.

visual.content:
identify and describe
Putting it together

Given a shape and where it ended up, work out which move did it. Then write the description an examiner wants to read.

This final section works like the real paper: identify the move first, then describe it in full for the marks.

slides.title: The decision tree
slides.prompt: When you've got an object and its image, work through these four questions in order. Each "yes" or "no" narrows it down to one move.

visual.content:
Same size?
NO →
ENLARGEMENT
↓ YES
Orientation flipped?
YES →
REFLECTION
↓ NO
Every vertex shifts by same vector?
YES →
TRANSLATION
↓ NO
ROTATION

config.prompt: Blue maps to pink. Which transformation is it?

options.whyWrong: Reflection would flip orientation. The triangles point the same way here.
Rotation changes the orientation. Both look the same here.
The triangles are the same size. No enlargement.

config.successText: Same shape, same size, same orientation. That's a translation.

config.prompt: Same diagram. Write the full answer, the way the paper wants it.

options.whyWrong: The everyday word earns nothing. The proper name is translation.
Pink is higher up the page than blue. Up means a positive bottom number.
A negative top number means left, but pink is to the right of blue.
Pink sits up and to the right of blue, so both numbers are positive.

config.successText: Translation by $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$. You named the move and gave the column vector, which is both marks.

config.prompt: Triangle $T$ has vertices $A(1, 1), B(4, 1), C(1, 3)$. Reflect $T$ in $y = x$. Which is the image $T_1$?

options.whyWrong: That's a $180°$ rotation, not a reflection in $y = x$.
That's a reflection in the $x$-axis. Wrong mirror.
That's a reflection in the $y$-axis.

config.prompt: Rotate $T_1\ (A_1(1,1), B_1(1,4), C_1(3,1))$ by $90°$ clockwise about the origin. Image $T_2$?

options.whyWrong: That's anticlockwise: $(x,y) \to (-y,x)$. The question asks clockwise.
That's a $180°$ rotation, not $90°$.
That's no rotation. The triangle did rotate $90°$ clockwise.

config.prompt: Describe the single transformation that maps $T$ straight onto $T_2$.

options.whyWrong: A $180°$ rotation would flip both signs. Here only the $y$-coordinates have flipped.
Check the corners: $(1, 3)$ dropped six squares but $(1, 1)$ dropped only two, so this is not one slide.
$x = 0$ would flip the $x$-coordinates, but they are unchanged here.
Reflecting in $y = x$ swaps the coordinates. Nothing is swapped here.

config.successText: Reflection in the line $y = 0$. Every $y$-coordinate flips sign while $x$ stays put, and that mirror is the $x$-axis.

interaction.hint: Say the three pieces in order: the move, the angle with its direction, then the centre.

options.whyWrong: Try to place a single mirror between blue and pink and the corners never match up.
Both triangles are the same size, so nothing has been scaled.
Watch corner $(5, 1)$: it swings up and over to $(-1, 5)$, which is against the clock.
Three quarter-turns anticlockwise equals one quarter-turn clockwise, and that lands the triangle below the axis.
A rotation about $(1, 1)$ would leave that point fixed and land the image somewhere else. Check with one corner.
$(-1, 2)$ is where a corner landed, not the point everything turned around.

config.successText: Rotation, $90°$ anticlockwise, centre $(0, 0)$. That is the full three-mark sentence, written the way the examiner reads it.

slides.title: You can now describe any single move
slides.prompt: Four transformations. Four mark-scheme patterns. Plus the rules for combining them.
bullets: Name the move first, then give its details.
Two parallel mirrors combine into a translation, and two intersecting mirrors combine into a rotation.
To combine two translations, add their column vectors.
Lengths scale by $k$, areas by $k^2$, volumes by $k^3$.
